stops.name: La Laguna, Juan Huallparrimachi joins the household
stops.campa: A cholo youth of uncommon gift comes into the Padilla camp: Juan Huallparrimachi, natural son of the former governor of Potosí, Francisco de Paula Sanz, and an indigenous mother, a poet in Quechua and a born soldier both. Manuel makes him lieutenant; Juana, childless in her heart for the sons she has had to hide away with distant caretakers, treats him as her own. He trains her boys in bow and lance and huaraca when he can reach them, scouts the royalist columns, and becomes within months indispensable to the republiqueta's survival, the nearest thing to a fourth Padilla child the war allows her to raise.

stops.name: Jujuy, the Éxodo Jujeño
stops.campa: As Belgrano empties Jujuy before the royalist advance, ordering the whole province south in a single column of carts, cattle, and refugees and burning what cannot be carried, the guerrillas of the republiquetas harry the Spanish rear from the north, buying the retreating army its margin. Padilla's riders strike supply trains and isolated pickets across the puna; Juana organizes the camp's stores and its wounded, unseen by Belgrano's staff but already known by name to the officers who pass word up the line that a woman commands alongside Padilla in Upper Peru, and commands well.

stops.name: Potosí, reunion under Belgrano's banner
stops.campa: Belgrano's Second Auxiliary Expedition enters Potosí in triumph after Salta and Tucumán, and here, after long separation, Juana and Manuel present themselves and their irregulars to the general's headquarters in the Villa Imperial. Belgrano, who values discipline as much as courage, is struck by the ten thousand indigenous militia the Padillas can call to arms on the strength of reputation alone, and by the woman who has organized a corps she calls the Leales, the Loyal Ones, drilled from manuals he himself supplies. He folds the republiqueta's forces into his order of battle. Juana is no longer an irregular; she is an officer of the Army of the North in fact, if not yet in commission.

stops.name: Pampa de Vilcapugio, the battle lost while winning
stops.campa: On the high plateau of Vilcapugio, Belgrano's army breaks Pezuela's center and believes the day won, only for a false report of retreat and a collapse of the reserve to turn triumph into rout within the hour. Juana's Leales, posted to the flank, hold their ground longer than most and cover the disordered withdrawal of units that panic before they do. She sees, in the space of an afternoon, how quickly a battle already won can be lost to confusion rather than to the enemy, a lesson she will not forget in the guerrilla war she returns to fight on her own ground.

stops.name: Ayohúma, the Leales and the sabre of Belgrano
stops.campa: On the plain of Ayohúma, whose old name means head of the dead, Pezuela's guns dominate from the heights and the rebuilt patriot army is broken a second time. Juana commands the right flank with her Battalion of the Leales under Cornelio Zelaya, and holds it under fire alongside María Remedios del Valle, the Black captain the soldiers already call Madre de la Patria. The army is lost, but Belgrano, watching the two women's companies fight to the last order, does not forget it: for this day, and for Ayohúma's discipline in ruin, he will within three years give Juana the sabre that carried him through Salta, Tucumán, and the Jujuy exodus.

stops.name: Chuquisaca province, the ruse against Carvallo
stops.campa: Carvallo, a royalist official under the notorious Sánchez de Velasco, has made a trade of extorting and executing indigenous villagers across the province. Padilla and the guerrilla chief José Ignacio Zárate capture Sánchez de Velasco outright; when royalist troops seize Padilla and Zárate in reprisal and begin to torture them, Juana and Huallparrimachi save them by cunning rather than force, shouting Zárate's feared name through the dark until the drunk, panicked guards believe his whole company has returned and abandon the prisoners rather than face him. Padilla and Zárate walk free before dawn, saved by two voices in the dark.

stops.name: Cerro de las Carretas, the death of Huallparrimachi
stops.campa: A bribed guide leads royalist Colonel Sebastián Benavente to the guerrilla camp at Cerro de las Carretas, two leagues from Tarabuco, and three days of fighting follow among the crags. In the worst of it a cannon-shot aimed at Juana is intercepted by Huallparrimachi's own body; he throws himself into its path and dies of the wound, the poet-lieutenant she had raised as a son given for the mother who raised him. The camp holds the ground despite the loss, and the action draws new recruits to the republiqueta even as it costs Juana one of the people she loved best in the war.

stops.name: Valle de Segura, the deaths of the children
stops.campa: In the fever-ridden lowlands of the Valle de Segura, where the republiqueta shelters its noncombatants, malaria moves through the Padilla children one by one. Juana buries her sons Manuel and Mariano herself, in graves she cannot mark for fear of desecration, and rides to recover Juliana and Mercedes from royalist hands only to watch the same fever take them within days of the rescue. Four of her five children die this way, camp-born and camp-buried, casualties the official histories of battles never count. Afterward those who serve under her say she no longer spares a captured officer as she once did.

stops.name: Pintatora, birth in the field and the captured standard
stops.campa: The labor pains come on Juana at Pintatora with the sound of royalist cavalry already entering the camp; she gives birth to her fifth child, Luisa, within earshot of the alarm, by the bank of the Río Grande, in the ordinary violence of a guerrilla republic that keeps no separate peace for mothers. Hours later, the canon says, she is back among her troops, rallying the line and personally cutting down the standard-bearer of the retreating royalist company. Luisa will be the only one of the five children to outlive the war, carried through it in a saddle-basket while her mother fights.

stops.name: El Villar, the standard of La Hera
stops.campa: Leading thirty mounted fighters, several of them women of her own recruiting whom the countryside has taken to calling the Amazonas, Juana charges the forces of the Spanish general La Hera near El Villar and breaks them, capturing the royal standard with her own hand and recovering a store of muskets the republiqueta badly needs. The action is small in numbers and enormous in what it proves: that a column she personally leads, not merely organizes from the rear, can take a fortified position from regular Spanish troops. Five days later she will ride on to prove it again at Potosí's own mountain.

stops.name: Cerro Rico de Potosí, the assault on the silver mountain
stops.campa: Five days after El Villar, Juana leads a cavalry strike against the fortifications thrown up around the Cerro Rico itself, the cone-shaped mountain whose silver has paid for the entire Spanish empire's wars for three centuries. Her riders take the outer defenses and another royalist standard before withdrawing; the raid cannot hold the mountain, but it plants the republiqueta's flag, briefly, on the most valuable piece of ground in South America, within sight of the Casa de Moneda's own chimneys. Reports of the action, and of El Villar before it, are what finally reach Buenos Aires and change how Pueyrredón's government rates her.

stops.name: La Laguna, the commission and Belgrano's sabre delivered
stops.campa: A courier reaches the camp at La Laguna carrying the decree Juan Martín de Pueyrredón, Director Supremo of the United Provinces, has signed on 13 August 1816: Juana Azurduy, teniente coronel, commanding a division to be called the Decididos del Perú, entitled to wear the uniform of the rank. With the commission comes something Belgrano chooses to send in place of the standard-issue blade, his own personal sabre, the one that rode with him through Salta, Tucumán, and the Jujuy exodus and stood beside her at broken Ayohúma. It is the highest rank yet given a woman in the armies of the revolution.
